extracted.intended_audience: naturalists; evolutionary_biologists; scholars and readers studying sexual selection and evolutionary explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and heuristic principles for inferring whether a given trait (colouration, ornament, weapon, behaviour) in birds or mammals arose by sexual selection, natural selection (protection), or by inheritance/transmission patterns. Focuses on patterns of expression by sex, age, season, costliness, and use in courtship or combat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually-limited transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: "we must look to the law of sexually-limited transmission."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character (e.g., male colours) appears principally or exclusively in one sex despite both sexes having been exposed to the same conditions, consider sexually-limited transmission as the explanatory mechanism. Examples: male-only bright lower surfaces; males distinct while females dull.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait unlikely to be for protection indicates sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When a conspicuous trait 'can hardly serve in any case as a protection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a colouration or ornament does not plausibly aid concealment, defence, or other protective function (e.g., complete or partial blackness, brilliant plumes), sexual selection is a more probable cause. Example: blackness in certain male birds (blackbird, blackcock) is unlikely protective and therefore probably sexually selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments incurred at a survival cost point to sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Brilliant colours and ornaments have 'been acquired in not a few cases at the cost of increased danger from enemies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits that increase predation risk or impair other survival functions yet persist are evidence they were favored by mate choice or male competition. Use: treat high-cost, conspicuous traits as likely sexually selected unless a protective or other benefit is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments/display used during courtship indicate sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Males 'display their charms ... in the presence of the females' and courtship can be prolonged; ornaments are 'by far the commonest means' of charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait is shown primarily during courtship/display, or males have specialized display behaviours/structures, this supports a sexual-selection explanation. Examples: dances, song, elongated feathers, wattles, plumes used in display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age- and season-limited expression suggests sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain plumage or ornaments 'become white only at maturity' or are 'developed only during the summer'; young and winter-plumaged adults differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits that appear only at maturity or only during the breeding season (or are more vivid then) are likely nuptial characters shaped by sexual selection. Use as diagnostic evidence: maturity- or season-linked onset of ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty or 'changes of fashion' can be sexually attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere novelty, or slight changes for the sake of change, 'have sometimes acted on female birds as a charm'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small or novel deviations from ancestral patterns can be favoured if they appeal to mate preferences; treat apparently capricious or fashion-like traits as potentially sexually selected. Examples: subtle shifts in collar colour among parrots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of taste (preference) via habit allows long-term sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste 'depends much on habit' and need not be so fluctuating as to prevent long-term selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating plausibility of sustained sexual selection, consider that preferences can be stable over many generations through habit or cultural-like continuity; objections based solely on presumed fickleness of taste are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative similarity of females implies male-driven divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: In almost every genus where the sexes differ, 'the males differ much more from one another than do the females'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When females of closely related species are similar but males differ markedly, interpret this as evidence that sexual selection has driven male divergence while females remained conserved—use comparative pattern across related species as diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared environment but sexual dimorphism argues against direct conditions-of-life causes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They are not due to the direct and definite action of the conditions of life, because the females have been exposed to the same conditions, and yet often differ from the males to an extreme degree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both sexes experience the same ecological conditions but show marked differences, do not attribute differences to direct environmental effects; consider sexual selection or differences in transmission instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission rules (sex, age, season) determine expression patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of inheritance 'appear to have determined whether the characters acquired by the males ... have been transmitted to the males alone or to both sexes, either permanently, or periodically during certain seasons of the year.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how inheritance modes (equal transmission, sexually-limited transmission, age-limited transmission) can explain observed trait distributions: e.g., traits transmitted equally -> both sexes resemble; sex-limited -> only one sex modified; age-limited -> adults but not young modified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-life variation preserved for male ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations arising 'late in life have so often been preserved for the ornamentation of the males; the females and the young being left almost unaffected'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a trait appears late in ontogeny (after juvenile phase) and is costly for young, natural selection may purge it in juveniles while sexual selection preserves it in reproducing adults—use timing of variation onset to infer selective regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male weapons and the 'law of battle' indicate sexual selection by male–male competition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'With mammals the male appears to win the female much more through the law of battle than through the display of his charms.' Examples: horns, tusks, enlarged canines, spurs, scars from fights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of specialised fighting structures (horns, tusks, enlarged canines, spurs) concentrated in males and coupled with observed male–male combat strongly supports sexual selection via competition. Evidence: scars, locked horns, fighting behaviours, sexual-season agonisticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or reduction of weapons in females despite potential utility implies sex-limited selection/transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: 'it is surprising that they are so poorly developed, or quite absent, in the females of so many animals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If females lack weapons present in males even though such weapons could be useful, infer that these weapons evolved primarily through male–male competition and are sex-limited by inheritance or by selection acting to eliminate them in females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phylogenetic and ontogenetic evidence (juvenile plumage as record) to infer ancestral states
rubrics_metrics.description: As the young of many species are little modified in colour 'we are enabled to form some judgment with respect to the plumage of their early progenitors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use juvenile and seasonal plumage, and comparative phylogenetic patterns across related species, to reconstruct ancestral states and the sequence of changes (e.g., dark → white → slaty/golden-buff) and thereby infer sexual-selection-driven transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous colours facilitating mate-finding at distance can be sexually selected
rubrics_metrics.description: 'males and females could find each other much more easily, when made conspicuous ... so that these colours may possibly serve the same end as the call-notes of many land-birds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mate-locating benefits (in open habitats, oceanic species) when conspicuous coloration is present; such signaling may be favored by sexual selection for mutual recognition and mate attraction even if not used in close-range courtship.
